papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) rewards are notoriously difficult to design and control, often leading to the model learning unintended behaviors such as reward hacking. One potential solution is to monitor for reward hacking and penalize it when detected; however, training against a monitor could lead to evasive behavior, and our general understanding of how to apply monitors effectively during training is limited. To study how best to use monitors to mitigate reward hacking, we introduce and open source three realistic environments where Qwen3-4B reward hacks: a coding environment hackable via test overwriting, a medical chat environment hackable via sycophancy, and a biography generation environment hackable via hallucination. We first focus on the coding environment, where we find that: (1) models can learn to evade highly accurate monitors by exploiting systemic flaws in probes and LLM judges; (2) monitors that leak more learning signal during RL suppress reward hacking but are more often evaded; and (3) including easier problems in training can decrease reward hacking. We apply our findings to build better reward hacking monitors for the medical chat and biography generation environments that improve upon naive baselines to reduce reward hacking rates across seeds to before-training levels in some interventions. Our results demonstrate that our takeaways translate to new settings and that better monitor intervention designs are possible.

papers.title: CodeQuant2: Enhanced Outlier Mitigation and Adaptive Clustering for Low-Precision LRMs
papers.authors: Xingyu Liu, Xiangyang Yin, Tianhua Xia, Haiyu Wang et al.

papers.summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) improve task performance by generating longer intermediate reasoning traces, but this substantially increases inference costs and makes low-precision quantization increasingly important. However, aggressively quantized models often perform poorly on reasoning tasks. We observe larger activation fluctuations during the first decoding steps of reasoning. Calibration that omits these early states may miss their activation fluctuations. To address these reasoning-specific quantization challenges, we propose \textbf{CodeQuant2}, a clustering-based LUT quantization framework for low-precision large reasoning models. CodeQuant2 mitigates activation outliers with rotation and scaling, uses clustering to represent non-uniform weight distributions, and adapts codebook sizes to the quantization difficulty of each layer. Guided by our observation of reasoning-time activation behavior, CodeQuant2 further improves calibration sample selection to better match actual decoding statistics. Combined with our customized LUT CUDA kernel, CodeQuant2 delivers substantial accuracy improvements on reasoning benchmarks while achieving up to $2.85\times$ speedup over BF16.

papers.title: Assessing the Impact of Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Algorithmic Problem-Solving
papers.authors: Gabriel Souza Baggio, Gabriel Machado Lunardi, Guilherme Medeiros Machado, Subhankar Maity et al.

papers.summary: Competitive programming problems pose distinctive challenges for Large Language Models, as they demand not only proficient code generation but also advanced algorithmic reasoning. This study presents a Retrieval-Augmented Generation approach specifically designed to enhance the capacity of Large Language Models to address such problems. Our approach integrates an embedding-based retrieval mechanism and a similarity search algorithm to identify analogous problems within a knowledge database, employing a dynamically adjusted threshold to mitigate retrieval noise. We conducted an evaluation using the CodeContests dataset, focusing on the test split problems that exhibit similarity to instances from the training split. The experimental framework considered three conditions: (i) problems provided solely with their original descriptions, (ii) problems supplemented with randomly selected examples from the training split, and (iii) problems augmented with similar examples retrieved through the proposed method. In addition, we incorporated a Min-K membership inference analysis to examine whether the generated code solutions were influenced by potential memorization of training data within the evaluated Large Language Models. This complementary perspective enables a deeper understanding of model behavior by distinguishing genuine generalization through retrieval from implicit recall of pretraining samples. Performance was assessed using both pass rates and the CodeForces Elo rating of the problems. The results provide empirical evidence that similarity-based retrieval substantially enhances Large Language Models performance in competitive programming scenarios, offering an scalable framework for improving code generation in algorithmic problem-solving contexts.

papers.authors: Peter Belcak, Greg Heinrich, Saurav Muralidharan, Shizhe Diao et al.

papers.summary: Large language models reinvent the wheel all the time. They conflate task-solving with the execution of the solutions, which forces them to solve every problem from scratch. We show that once a task has been reasoned through, the application of its solution to a new problem instance can be done very efficiently and with little involvement from language models. We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a method for constructing robust CPU-executable agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces. ARCs show on-par performance with frontier LLMs across a range of difficult mathematical and scientific tasks, are fully explainable, continually trainable, robust to input perturbations, and 16-291x cheaper to invoke than the source model.

papers.title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.authors: Andy Arditi, Oscar Obeso, Aaquib Syed, Daniel Paleka et al.
papers.what: [Conference] Conversational large language models are fine-tuned for both instruction-following and safety, resulting in models that obey benign requests but refuse harmful ones. While this refusal behavior is widespread across chat models, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood.
papers.summary: Conversational large language models are fine-tuned for both instruction-following and safety, resulting in models that obey benign requests but refuse harmful ones. While this refusal behavior is widespread across chat models, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, across 13 popular open-source chat models up to 72B parameters in size. Specifically, for each model, we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model's residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions, while adding this direction elicits refusal on even harmless instructions. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel white-box jailbreak method that surgically disables refusal with minimal effect on other capabilities. Finally, we mechanistically analyze how adversarial suffixes suppress propagation of the refusal-mediating direction. Our findings underscore the brittleness of current safety fine-tuning methods. More broadly, our work showcases how an understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical methods for controlling model behavior.

papers.title: Instant Payments After a Betting Ban: Evidence from Brazil
papers.what: [Explore] Brazil has been facing major problems with delinquency, household debt, high interest rates, consumption, and access to credit. Betting has emerged in public debate as a possible contributing factor. On September 25, 2026, the federal government banned betting nationwide. We inve
papers.summary: Brazil has been facing major problems with delinquency, household debt, high interest rates, consumption, and access to credit. Betting has emerged in public debate as a possible contributing factor. On September 25, 2026, the federal government banned betting nationwide. We investigate how the ban affected instant payments (Pix). Our main finding, under the linear-trend specification, is that cumulative transaction counts over 37 days were approximately 8.37% below forecast, while settlement values were 10.83% lower. Both deviations were statistically significant under this specification.

papers.title: Effects of a Nuclear Detonation in Low Earth Orbit
papers.authors: Zachary Petersen, Hong Qin, Sarah Thiele, Sébastien Philippe
papers.what: [Explore] More than 13,000 satellites operate in low Earth orbit (LEO), and concern has grown that nuclear weapons could be used in space to target them. papers.summary: More than 13,000 satellites operate in low Earth orbit (LEO), and concern has grown that nuclear weapons could be used in space to target them. Beyond the initial X-ray burst, electrons released by radioactive fission products can become trapped in Earth's magnetic field, repeatedly exposing satellites as an artificial radiation belt. Here we couple prompt radiation, electron trapping and belt evolution to satellite failures, collisions and atmospheric drag. For a 1-Mt detonation at 500km over the South Atlantic, repeated belt exposure disables approximately 98% of modeled satellites within one week in our central case. Tripling the assumed radiation tolerance delays widespread failure by only days: approximately 97% are still disabled within two weeks. The loss of maneuverability sharply increases collision risk, with approximately 20 collisions expected within two years. Drag removes many disabled spacecraft from lower altitudes, but replacement satellites could remain exposed to radiation and debris for years. These findings show how a single detonation could devastate orbital infrastructure and support efforts to prevent the deployment and use of nuclear weapons in space.
